title: Delhi Just Banned New Petrol Two-Wheelers From 2028. Only Electric Vehicles Will Be Registered.
excerpt: India's capital launches its most aggressive EV policy yet — ₹15,000 crore in incentives, 30,000 charging points, and a hard deadline that phases out fossil-fuel two-wheelers and auto-rickshaws.
body:
India's capital just drew a line in the asphalt. Starting this week, Delhi's new Electric Vehicle Policy 2026 is in effect, and it carries a radical mandate: by April 2028, not a single new petrol or CNG-powered two-wheeler will be eligible for registration in the city. Auto-rickshaws face the same deadline six months earlier — only electric models will be registered from January 2027.

Chief Minister Rekha Gupta announced the policy as a "historic step toward effectively controlling vehicular pollution in the capital." The Delhi Cabinet approved the plan on June 29, Lieutenant Governor Taranjit Singh Sandhu gave final clearance, and the policy took effect on July 1.

**The Numbers Behind the Mandate**

Delhi plans to invest approximately ₹15,000 crore ($1.6 billion) over four years on incentives, charging infrastructure, and the broader EV ecosystem. The government has set a target that would stretch the imagination of most cities worldwide: 95% of all new vehicle registrations in Delhi should be electric by 2027.

The incentive structure is designed to make the switch financially compelling. Electric cars priced under ₹30 lakh ($32,000) will receive a full exemption from road tax and registration fees. Electric two-wheelers get purchase incentives of up to ₹30,000 ($320) in the first year, tapering to ₹10,000 by the third year. Three-wheelers get up to ₹50,000, and electric commercial trucks up to ₹1 lakh.

A scrappage programme sweetens the deal further. Owners who retire BS-IV or older four-wheelers and switch to electric can claim up to ₹1 lakh. Two-wheeler scrappage incentives start at ₹10,000. Over ₹1,500 crore has been earmarked for these scrappage benefits alone.

**Hybrids Are Out**

In a notable departure from the draft policy released in April, the final version excludes hybrid vehicles entirely. No subsidies, no tax waivers, no incentives. It is a bet on full electrification, rejecting the halfway measure that automakers like Toyota and Maruti Suzuki have been lobbying for across India.

**30,000 Charging Points**

The government plans to install more than 30,000 public EV charging points across the city during the policy period, funded through the central government's PM e-Drive Scheme and Delhi's own budget. Charging stations will be placed at markets, workplaces, and high-traffic public locations, while provisions for residential charging meters are also being developed.

School operators face their own mandate — at least 10% of their bus fleet must be electric within two years, rising to 30% by March 2030.

**Why This Matters Beyond Delhi**

The policy is significant because it targets the vehicle categories that pollute the most. Government data shows commercial goods vehicles account for about 33% of vehicular pollution in Delhi, while two-wheelers and three-wheelers contribute another 46%. Together, these categories produce nearly four-fifths of the city's vehicle-related emissions — and all three are now on a mandatory electrification timeline.

Delhi has tried before. Partial restrictions on fossil fuel transport and water trucks spraying mist to cut smog have failed to make a noticeable dent. The city's PM 2.5 levels have exceeded 300 micrograms per cubic meter — 20 times the World Health Organization's recommended daily maximum. A *Lancet Planetary Health* study estimated 3.8 million deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to air pollution.

**The Diaspora Connection**

For the millions of NRIs who visit Delhi every winter — and dread the annual smog season — this policy represents the most aggressive attempt yet to tackle the problem at its source. It also opens investment opportunities: Delhi expects the policy to attract investments across electric mobility, battery manufacturing, charging infrastructure, and recycling facilities.

Existing petrol and CNG vehicles are not affected by the registration bans. But the direction is unmistakable. Delhi is wagering that the economics of electric mobility have tipped far enough that mandates will accelerate adoption rather than strangle it.

The policy remains in force until March 31, 2030.

*Sources: Delhi Government notification, Rushlane, Phys.org, Capital Market*
